Good morning. The high-level meeting of the General Assembly to commemorate the 25th anniversary of the adoption of the Durban Declaration and Programme of Action is called to order. I warmly welcome all of you to this high-level meeting convened to mark the 25th anniversary of the adoption of the Durban Declaration This high-level meeting is held on the theme, mobilizing global public support for the full and effective implementation of the Durban Declaration and Programme of Action in accordance with General Assembly resolution 80/193 of 15 December 2025 and 80/299 of 28 July 2026. Allow me now to make a statement as President of the General Assembly. Your Excellency, Minister of International Relations and Cooperation of South Africa; Your Excellency, Mr. Secretary-General; Excellencies; distinguished delegates; 25 years ago, the international community came together in Durban with a shared conviction that racism is an assault on human dignity that racial discrimination entrenches injustice and inequality, and that xenophobia and related intolerance threaten peace within and among nations. The Durban Declaration and Program of Action was born in South Africa, a heroic nation whose people proved that institutionalized racism can be overcome. Durban drew strength from that struggle. It also confronted the enduring legacies of slavery and the slave trade, including the transatlantic slave trade, colonialism, apartheid, and genocide. Durban, therefore, went beyond condemning prejudice. It confronted racism as a structural force. It called for stronger laws and institutions, national action plans, education, disaggregated data, equal participation, justice, remedies, and international cooperation. It placed affected communities at the center and remains today the most comprehensive global framework to combat systemic racism, racial discrimination, xenophobia, and related intolerance. The 25th anniversary, which we mark today, calls for renewed vigilance to uphold its historic tenets. Excellencies, the fight against racism, racial discrimination, xenophobia and related intolerance is not a matter of choice. It's a core obligation rooted in the UN Charter, international human rights law, and the commitments made in Durban. It's a responsibility we owe to every person everywhere, and we must deliver on it. Yet, we are falling short. The Committee on the Elimination of Racial Discrimination reports that 78 of the Convention's 182 States parties are significantly behind in their reporting, some by decades. This is more than a reporting gap; it is an accountability gap. We cannot remedy inequalities we refuse to examine. We cannot dismantle discrimination we fail to measure, and we cannot fulfill commitments without resources, monitoring, and political will. Excellencies, the political declaration before us calls for national action plans, comprehensive laws, independent human rights institutions, effective remedies, education, and meaningful participation by affected communities. We must translate those commitments into action. That means investigating racist acts impartially, promptly, and thoroughly. It means ending impunity, prohibiting racial profiling, and ensuring justice and adequate reparation for victims. It means collecting disaggregated data consistent with human rights and national law to expose discrimination hidden by averages. And it means confronting historical injustice through acknowledgement, remembrance, and meaningful reparatory justice that restores dignity and addresses continuing inequalities. Excellencies, racism does not stand still. It adapts to changing social, political, and technological realities. It can be embedded in institutions, concealed in supposedly neutral procedures, reproduced through biased data sets and amplified by digital platforms that reward outrage and division. Artificial intelligence can expand opportunity, but poorly and unguarded systems can reproduce structural inequalities and spread lies and hatred at unprecedented speed and scale. We need safeguards throughout the technological life cycle, representative data, transparency, human oversight, accountability, and remedies. Innovation must advance equality, not automate discrimination. We must respond firmly to hate speech, disinformation, Islamophobia, Christianophobia, anti-Semitism, anti-Black racism, anti-Asian racism, xenophobia, discrimination against Indigenous peoples and Roma, and towards minorities, migrants, refugees, women and girls. No community should have to live in fear because of its race, ethnicity, national origin, religion or belief. No digital platform should be allowed to profit from hatred without accountability. Excellencies, to succeed, we must strengthen national action, deepen regional cooperation, and reinforce global solidarity, taking stock of where gains have been made and where new approaches are needed. And we must place young people, our standard bearers, at the heart of our efforts. I'm honored to have youth representatives with us today. Across the world, young people are using their voices and, importantly, their digital skills to push back against prejudice, challenge harmful narratives, promote inclusion, and build more just and inclusive societies. They are exposing discrimination and using digital skills to build inclusive societies. We must listen. Invest in their leadership and protect them, and include them meaningfully in designing and monitoring anti-racism policies. As Nelson Mandela reminded us, no one is born hating another person because of the color of his skin or his background or religion. Hatred is learned, but so are respect, solidarity, and our shared humanity. Excellencies, this anniversary must mobilize public support, not merely commemorate Durban. We must move from declarations to funded national action plans, from promises to measurable results, from incomplete data to accountability, from impunity to justice, and from acknowledgment of historical wrongs to dignity, healing, and meaningful repair. Today, as we reflect on 25 years since Durban, let us urgently renew our political will together. Let us defend the equal worth of every human being. Let us build societies where diversity is valued as a source of strength. And let us make equality and non-discrimination an enduring reality for every person, everywhere. In larger freedom, in equal dignity and in solidarity with all. The mandate is clear, the responsibility is shared, and the time for action is now. I thank you. I now have the honor to invite the Secretary General of the United Nations, His Excellency Antonio Guterres, to make a statement. You have the floor, sir.

Mr. President of the General Assembly, Excellencies, dear friends, the United Nations is guided by a simple yet profound purpose: to help build a more peaceful, just and equal world where the dignity and rights of every person is upheld. This is a moral imperative and a shared responsibility. Member States have made a solemn pledge to combat racism, to eradicate discrimination in all its forms, and to advance the dignity, human rights and equality of all those affected by racism, racial discrimination, xenophobia and related intolerance. This mission is even more urgent today than when the Durban Declaration and Programme of Action was adopted 25 years ago. As we see around the world, racism continues to poison societies, deepen inequalities and deny people their fundamental rights and freedoms. It is deeply rooted in the entrenched legacies of colonialism, enslavement, and oppression. And it takes many forms, from economic, social, and political inequalities within and across continents. The laws, policies, and institutions that discriminate against people because of their race, religion, color, descent, or national or ethnic origin, To the daily denial of dignity, rights, safety, and equal opportunity faced by people of African descent, indigenous peoples, migrants, refugees, and minorities. To digital tools and technologies that are amplifying the spread of hate speech and disinformation, perpetuating lies and harmful stereotypes, and fueling violence and abuse. Excellencies, The antidote to these poisons is unity and tangible action. Governments must strengthen and effectively implement anti-discrimination and equality laws, and the institutions that enforce them. They must also spare no effort to dismantle systemic discrimination and invest in inclusive and equal societies. While governments must take the lead, everyone has a role to play. Businesses, must respect the right to equality and non-discrimination by preventing direct and indirect discrimination and creating workplaces where all people can contribute their talents and ideas. Technology companies must identify, mitigate, and address bias in artificial intelligence systems and ensure that digital technologies advance equality, inclusion, and digital justice rather than undermine them.

Excellencies, as your panel discussion will highlight, younger generations are bringing the spirit for dignity, justice, and equality into the spaces where their futures are being decided in classrooms, communities, workplaces, technology labs, and digital platforms. As we look ahead, The world must confront the enduring consequences of slavery, colonialism, and racial discrimination through concrete measures to deliver reparatory justice grounded in international human rights law. We must also make the second International Decade for People of African Descent a decade of concrete change. And we need to see the universal ratification and full implementation of the International Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Racial Discrimination. Excellencies, today and every day, let us take a stand. Together, let us fight for the dignity, rights, and belonging of all people. Together, let us reject injustice. Together, let us build societies where racism and discrimination have no place, today and for all time. Thank you.

Thank you, Mr. President of the General Assembly, Excellencies, dear colleagues and friends. 25 years since the adoption of the Durban Declaration and Programme of Action, Millions of people still experience racism as a daily reality, in opportunities denied and discrimination across all spheres of life. According to the 2026 Global Progress Report on Sustainable Development Goal 16, reports of discriminations are rising globally. Nearly one in five people across the world report having experienced discrimination in the past 12 months. Overall, race, color, ethnicity, and socioeconomic status are the most commonly cited reasons for discrimination. These are not abstract statistics. They speak to lived realities. Racial discrimination continues to shape people's experiences in schools, workplaces, hospitals and housing, in interactions with law enforcement, at borders and across criminal justice systems. The Durban Declaration and Programme of Action challenged us to change this. It recognized the breadth of groups facing racism. people of African descent, indigenous peoples, Roma, refugees, asylum seekers and internally displaced people, minorities and many others, often compounded by other factors such as sex, gender, disability, migration status, ethnicity, religion of belief or poverty. This represents millions of people worldwide. Today, our responsibility is not simply to reaffirm the promise of Durban, but to turn that promise into action and real impact. Over the past 25 years, progress has been made. Laws have changed. Institutions have been established. Anti-racism movements have transformed public debate. At a time when this progress is threatened and we witness rollback in some countries, this anniversary must also be a moment of truth. Mr. President, the Durban Declaration recognized a fundamental idea. Inequalities cannot be understood or addressed without reference to the past. The declaration recognized that slavery, the slave trade, apartheid, colonialism, and genocide were among the major sources and manifestation of racism and racial discrimination. It recognized that African and people of African descent, Asians and people of Asian descent, and indigenous peoples were victims of these acts and continue to be victims of their consequences. This is why reparatory justice for legacies of the past is so essential. It is about truth seeking, acknowledgement and apologies, education and memorialization, compensation, restitution of heritage, medical and psychological support, and ensuring that victims and affected communities help determine what reparatory justice should look like. For Africans and people of African descent, reparatory justice is key to dismantle systemic racism and transforming the present and future. Excellencies, 25 years after Durban, the central challenge is implementation. We need a shift from commitments to equality to measure racial equality. To make this a reality, five priorities demand urgent action. First, states need to adopt and effectively implement comprehensive national laws, policies and action plans against racial discrimination with measurable targets, adequate resources and mechanisms for monitoring and accountability. Second, we need better data. States need to collect and publish data disaggregated by race or ethnic origin and other factors consistent with human rights and privacy safeguards. Third, we need accountability and remedy. Victims of racial discrimination must be able to obtain justice. Allegations of racial profiling, discriminatory policing, and racist violence need to be effectively investigated and those responsible held accountable. Fourth, we need to advance reparatory justice, grounded in international human rights law and developed with the full and meaningful participation of affected communities. Finally, we need to ensure that the digital transformation advances equally rather than undermines it. State and companies should assess and address racial bias in artificial intelligence and algorithm systems, ensure meaningful transparency and accountability, and provide effective remedies where discrimination occurs. Across all of this, meaningful and inclusive participation of affected people and civil society, particularly young people, must be central. The second International Decade for People of African Descent is an opportunity for concrete steps to dismantling the structures that continue to produce racial inequality. The UN Human Rights Office is an ally in these efforts. We advocate for the implementation of Durban Declaration and we work with the states, regional bodies, national institutions, civil society and affected communities to combat racial discrimination, xenophobia and related intolerance. Mr. President, 25 years ago, the Durban Declaration articulated an ambitious vision. a world in which equality and dignity are not determined by race, color, descent, or national or ethnic origin. That vision remains unfulfilled. Let this anniversary be a call to action, to turn commitments into real equality. Durban gave us the roadmap. What is needed now is the political will to act. Thank you.

I thank the Assistant Secretary-General for Human Rights. I now invite His Excellency Ronald Lamola, Minister of International Relations and Cooperation of South Africa, to make a statement. You have the floor, sir.

Thank you very much, President of the General Assembly, the Secretary-General of the United Nations, the United Nations Representative High Commissioner for Human Rights, Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen. 25 years ago, the world converged on our shores in Durban, South Africa, for the World Conference Against Racism, Racial Discrimination, Xenophobia and Related Intolerance. At the opening of that conference, the then President of the Republic of South Africa, Thabo Mbeki, said the gathering heralded a new era of internationalism. It was an internationalism marked by determination to unite in action to repair the gross damage that was caused in the past. From that conference came a landmark framework and a roadmap with a clear commitment to confront the legacies of slavery, colonialism, apartheid, and racial discrimination. The Durban Declaration and the Programme of Action marked a pivotal moment in the international community's commitment to build a world rooted in equality, dignity and justice. It also recognized that racism and related intolerance will not be defeated through state action alone. Laws and independent institutions are needed to combat discrimination and policies to uplift those on the receiving end of discriminations are very critical. But also civil society, communities and ordinary people have a pivotal role in changing these realities. Therefore, Durban was a major success. It set the norms and gave the world a programme to address one of the historical and perennial scourges facing the world. This declaration and programme of action was adopted in a challenging global context. The conference was marked by fierce debate, courage and willingness to confront uncomfortable truths about the past and its stubborn effects. 25 years later, the global environment is not less challenging. Racism persists. Xenophobia and related intolerance are finding renewed expression, worsened by digital platforms, algorithms and some of the prejudices that still exist in some of our societies. Gains in gender equalities are also under threat. Measures aimed at to redress and anti-racism are facing a backlash and are sometimes portrayed as discriminatory in themselves. This fraught context makes our renewed commitment to the Durban Declaration even more pressing. Contemporary racism against Africans and people of African descent is still embedded in institutions, systems, and practices that govern human affairs across the globe. This is why we must strengthen our collective efforts, Excellencies. Inequality and insecurity provide fertile ground for resentment and polarization. The global hardening of attitudes towards migrants, who are often a scapegoat for socioeconomic hardships, is also more reason for us to push for more cooperative ways of addressing migration pressures. The management of irregular migrations must be the responsibility of all states and states alone. Failure to cooperate leaves the doors wide open for actors whose conduct runs counter to the principles of equality, dignity, and human solidarity that we stand for. In fact, such actors see an opportunity to return to the past to work hard to fragment our societies into racial and ethnic divides. But even in these challenging moments, there is reason for hope. With the Ghana's leadership and the support of the African Union, this General Assembly recently adopted a declaration of the trafficking of enslaved Africans and the racialized chattel enslavement of Africans as the gravest crime against humanity. This gives renewed force to the demand for reparative justice. With Togo's stewardship and the backing of the African Union, the UN General Assembly recently adopted a resolution to correct the map, rebalancing global cartographic representation and promoting a more equitable representation of the world's region. This will go a long way in correcting distortions which have long depicted Africa as smaller than it is. These advances remind us that past wrongs will not right themselves, historical distortions do not correct themselves, and progress is always a product of a struggle, and that we need to remain resilient to move forward in building societies free of racism, xenophobia, and related intolerance. Today, we renew our call on states to address the legacies of the past, including through formal apologies, through telling reparations and the return of cultural artifacts to countries of origin. We welcome the progress towards the UN Declaration on the Human Rights of People of African Descent. This anniversary should mark a turning point in protecting human rights, reducing inequality, and advancing inclusive development. The envisaged UN declaration must give practical effect to second international decade and serve as a framework for redressing past injustices. As we mark 25 years of the declaration, we should redouble our efforts to bridge the gulf between the promise of laws and international commitments and the reality citizens and non-citizens experience on their daily lives. Excellencies, South Africa acknowledges and welcomes the political declaration marking the 25th anniversary of the Durban Declaration. In particular, we hope that all States will establish or strengthen independent national human rights institutions. These institutions should play a pivotal role in monitoring and evaluating the implementation of the declaration. The declaration call upon us to marshal political will at every level and to build momentum that cannot be turned back. At home, in our regions and across the world. we will take concrete and measurable steps to fight racism, racial discrimination, xenophobia and related intolerance. 25 years ago, we recognized that Durban marked the beginning, not the end. The task of building a world free of racism, righting the wrongs of the past and restoring the human dignity of all is as much as ours today as it was for the generations that converged in Durban a quarter century ago. I thank you.
I thank the Minister of International Relations and Cooperation of South Africa. I now invite Ms. Marley Diaz, a representative from civil society, to make a statement.

Assistant Secretary-General for Human Rights, Member States, Excellencies, and colleagues, thank you for the opportunity to speak. I belong to a generation that has come of age in the years since this declaration was adopted. Many of us were never taught the histories that shaped the world we inherited, the systems that built our institutions, drew our borders, and determined whose story would be preserved. This anniversary is an invitation to remedy that, and a reminder that the work of teaching is a shared responsibility. To those who wrote and carry out this declaration every day, thank you. The theme of this meeting is mobilizing global public support. But before we can cultivate that support, I believe we must be candid about what stands in its way. The first obstacle is our reluctance to acknowledge that our systems have failed people. It is more comfortable to regard slavery, colonialism, discrimination, sexism, and xenophobia as chapters that we have closed. But as any reader knows, earlier chapters do not vanish when we turn the page. They shape every chapter that follows, and stories make little sense to someone who skips up. The declaration asks us to not skip ahead. We must read carefully to understand the story as a whole. Only then can we comprehend the way these legacies have endured in our institutions and shaped our daily lives. No country is free of racism, and we cannot dismantle what we are unwilling to examine honestly. That candor is the heart of this document. It is also what makes it so demanding to fulfill. States, delegations, and institutions are ultimately composed of people. Whether this declaration endures beyond this chamber depends on individuals here and in the communities you represent, resolving to carry it forward. I came to understand these truths through books. Books gave me language, offered me history, and a way to see myself. When I was 11, I started the #1000BlackGirlBooks because I could not find stories with girls like me as the main character while I was reading in school. What began as a search for 1,000 books has grown into a collection of more than 15,000. Along the way, I witnessed what happens when a child discovers herself on the page. She gains a vocabulary for what she is living through. And when other children encounter her story, they begin to comprehend a life unlike their own. That holds true for children of African descent, for indigenous children, for migrant children, and for every community this declaration recognizes. And it particularly holds true for girls. For when we educate a girl, we educate a community. With that in mind, I would like to make three requests. First, I ask that young people become a central part of how this declaration is carried out. The UN Youth Office and youth networks across the UN system are well placed to lead that work and to equip young people with the language to recognize inequity and confront it. We must also meet young people where they are. Many now encounter these histories online, often in fragments and without context. Our lives are still lived in physical communities, but our understanding of them is increasingly shaped in digital spaces. If we want young people to learn this history truthfully, We must be present in those spaces as well, with materials that are accurate, accessible, and designed for the ways they actually learn. Second, I ask that we encourage families alongside students. Families are the first institutions. Their actions shape our morals and our values. Families give children their first language for understanding the world. So long before a child opens up a history book, she learns from the people around her how to describe fairness, difference, and belonging. My own parents gave me words for what I noticed was missing from my bookshelf. The declaration recognizes that education begins within the family. Partnering with UNESCO, NGOs, and national education authorities to develop accessible materials for parents would help families pass on that language of equity with confidence, carry these conversations into the home, and embed them into the primary institutions shaping our everyday lives. Third, I ask that the communities help decide how this declaration is implemented. Nothing for us without us. Affected communities and young people in particular should be at the forefront of designing and evaluating program of action plans. People sustain communities that they help shape. We must write and rewrite the narratives of inequity by crafting new and better stories. The stories we tell can allow us to feel seen for the first time and allow others a glimpse into a life they have never lived. Transformation of that kind is seldom sudden. It is cultivated through small, deliberate acts of listening, learning, and unlearning, sustained over time and together. This declaration was written by people who hoped a generation like mine would inherit a more just world. It began with an honest acknowledgement that our foreparents had failed many of its people, and that we must give birth to new forms of justice. Today, we honour this history by continuing what it set in motion. We commit to learning our history together, telling it truthfully, and passing it on, so that every person has a reason to believe these commitments were made with them in mind. Let's write a new chapter together. Thank you.

Mr. President, 25 years ago in Durban, the international community made a solemn commitment to eliminate racism, racial discrimination, and related forms of intolerance, as well as the legal and institutional infrastructures that perpetuate and sustain them. Mr. President, The Deputy Secretary General, Excellencies, distinguished delegates. Nigeria aligns with the statement just delivered on behalf of the African group. The Silver Jubilee anniversary provides a unique opportunity to test talk of the progress achieved over the years and significant gaps that remain. Despite repeated commitments, racism and racial discrimination persist in many societies, while Africa and people of African descent continue to experience racial profiling, exclusion, and unequal treatment. Without doubt, the challenge is not the absence of an agreed framework, but the lack of sufficient resolve and concrete action to fully implement it. Mr. President, racism is also assuming new dimensions through emerging technologies, including artificial intelligence. While Nigeria recognizes AI's transformative potential and the significant opportunities it offers, we believe that without appropriate safeguards, its development and use could entrench existing biases and further exacerbate racial discrimination. Despite growing recognition of the link between AI and racial discrimination, this issue still lacks the universal attention and action needed to address it effectively. Earlier this year, the General Assembly adopted the resolution resolution 8250 declaring the trafficking of enslaved Africans and the racial channel enslavement of African as grif crime against humanity the legacies of slavery colonialism and historical injustice continue to shape present day inequalities addressing these legacies is not about reopening history but a necessary step to Justice Nigeria therefore calls on member state and other stakeholders to demonstrate concrete and genuine commitment to the full and effective implementation of the Doha Declaration and Programme of Action, including by building stronger national institutions, anti-discriminatory legislations, education and accountability. In conclusion, the success of this commemoration will not be measured by how many meetings we hold or resolutions we pass, but by meaningful impact and improvement in the lives of those who continue to experience racism and racial discrimination. Nigeria once again reaffirms its unequivocal commitment to this collective endeavor of combating racism, racial discrimination, xenophobia, and related forms of intolerance, and calls for renewed political will and international cooperation to make dignity, equality, and justice a lived reality for all. Thank you very much.
I thank the representative of Nigeria. Now I invite the representative of Ghana to make a statement.

Mr. President, Heads of Delegations, Excellencies, I commend the United Nations for this special commemoration. 25 years ago, the international community adopted a comprehensive framework to confront racism, racial discrimination, xenophobia, and related intolerance. The Durban Declaration affirmed our shared responsibility to address historical injustices and dismantle the structures that perpetuate inequality. This solemn day must bring us to a reckoning that what our world needs is decisive action, not more political declarations. It should be of great consternation to us all that 25 years after the Durban Declaration, we still need to remind some people that all men and women are created equal. 25 years after the Durban Declaration, we still have to proclaim that black lives matter. 25 years after Durban, we still seem to watch helplessly as a genocide unfolds in Palestine. with a two-state solution adopted by this Assembly becoming elusive each passing day. Twenty-five years after the Durban Declaration, but we cannot seem to save the people of Sudan. Twenty-five years after the Durban Declaration, but xenophobic attacks have become a recurring feature in South Africa. Twenty-five years after Durban, but this foremost multilateral organization, the United Nations, cannot uphold the principles of Durban by ensuring that Africa, a continent of 1.4 billion people, is guaranteed a permanent seat on the Security Council. The Durban commitments must become reality, not a mere slogan. President John Mahama of Ghana spoke a timeless truth when he stated in this hallowed chamber a few days ago that no race is superior and no nation is inferior. For Ghana, Durban's enduring significance also lies in its recognition that historical injustices continue to shape present inequalities. Reparatory justice is therefore essential to restoring dignity, addressing those inequalities, and building long-lasting trust. In paragraph 13 of the Durban Declaration, the world said slavery should have been a crime against humanity. This year, we removed the "should have been." by resoundingly correcting that historical injustice with the emphatic adoption of the Ghana-led landmark resolution declaring the trafficking of enslaved Africans as the gravest crime against humanity. Now we ask for what justice-- Thank you. Now we ask for what justice has always required, an apology that is sincere, return of our cultural heritage, repair for the harm that still lives on, and a promise, a real promise, that it will never, ever happen again. Ghana takes the firm view that there must be severe consequences for those who flagrantly violate the Durban Declaration and commit crimes against humanity. Ghana is therefore strongly opposed to attempts to abolish the International Criminal Court. The ICC should rather be strengthened.
I thank the distinguished representative of Ghana. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of the State of Palestine.

Mr. President. Twenty-five years ago, in Durban, the international community made a solemn commitment to confront racism, racial discrimination, xenophobia and related intolerance, and to uphold the dignity and equality of every human being. The State of Palestine welcomes today's adoption of this political declaration and its reaffirmation of the Durban Declaration and Programme of Action. For the Palestinian people, Durban carries particular significance. 25 years ago, the Durban Declaration expressed concern for the plight of the Palestinian people under foreign occupation. It recognized our inalienable right to self-determination and to the establishment of an independent state, while recognizing the right to security of all states in the region. Instead of realizing their right to self-determination and living in freedom and dignity in their independent state, the Palestinian people continue to endure an unlawful occupation and are confronted with genocide, continued ethnic cleansing, and apartheid. Today's declaration reminds us that colonialism, genocide, apartheid, and slavery have profound and lasting consequences, that racial discrimination, inequality, and displacement demand action, and that historical injustice cannot be overcome through remembrance alone. It requires justice and reparation. Durban must remain a commitment to action for the sake of the victims of the past and the present, and for future generations. We must reject racism and discrimination in all their forms and hatred directed against any people because of their identity, religion, origin or ordeal. We must uphold the universality of human rights without selectivity, exception or double standards. Mr. President, Palestine reaffirms its commitment to the Durban Declaration and Programme of Action and to equality, justice, and human dignity. 25 years after Durban, our responsibility is clear. The rights affirmed there must not merely be remembered. They must be realized for all peoples without exception, including the Palestinian people. And I thank you very much.
I thank the distinguished representative of the State of Palestine. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Cuba.

Mr. President, at the historic Durban Conference, the leader of the Cuban revolution, Fidel Castro Ruz, stated, and I quote, "Racism, racial discrimination, and xenophobia are not naturally instinctive reactions of human beings, but rather a social, cultural and political phenomenon born directly of wars, military conquests, slavery and the individual or collective exploitation of the weakest by the most powerful throughout the history of human society." End of quotation. Now we're seeing advances in xenophobia, discrimination, police brutality, racial profiling, intolerance, and supremacist ideologies, particularly in highly developed countries, targeting people of African descent, religious minorities, migrants, and indigenous peoples. The promise of societies free of discrimination remains on the horizon, as does the need for reparations for the horrors of slavery. The wealthiest nations, which benefited from centuries of conquest, colonization, and the transatlantic slave trade, refuse to assume their historical responsibilities. Some even opposed this Assembly's recognition of the slave trade as the most serious crime against humanity in history. At the same time, the international economic order perpetuates the exclusion of the vast majority and of the Global South. This is what our people have seen with the energy siege, the policy of maximum pressure with the tightened blockade, and continued threats of military aggression by the United States. Cuba is a proudly mixed-race nation whose African heritage and roots are an essential part of our identity. That is the source of much of our determination to be truly free, as well as our creativity and our unwavering resilience in the face of all threats. Thank you very much.
I thank the distinguished representative of Cuba. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Ethiopia.

Mr. President, my delegation aligns itself with the statement by Uruguay on behalf of the Group of 77 in China and Burkina Faso on behalf of the Africa Group. We appreciate the PGA for convening this high-level meeting on the 25th anniversary of the Durban Declaration and Programme of Action. The Universal Declaration of Human Rights sets for the protection of fundamental human rights and declares that all human beings are born free and equal. The Ethiopian Constitution adopted this universal principle. Ethiopia had joined hands with all like-minded states in the liberation of movements of African states from colonial subjugation and apartheid. This was informed by the spirit of Pan-Africanism and the victory of the Battle of Adwa, which sparked the drive to ending colonialism. The Pan-Africanism as shared common heritage also influenced the formation of the Organization of the African Unity in 1963. The 2001 World Conference Against Racism was a historic moment in the struggle for the equality of African peoples and people of African descent. Mr. President, on the 4th of October 1963, Emperor Haile Selassie of Ethiopia stood before the UN General Assembly and appealed to permanently abandon the false philosophy of racism. He urged for a world where the color of a human skin will be of no more significance than the color of human eyes, and that human rights should equally be guaranteed to all. Six decades after that appear, the world is struggling to find its way out of racially biased, socioeconomic, and political structures that impede the progress of all people. The people of Africa have endured inhuman treatment, beginning from the transatlantic slave trade, colonization, and all their misgivings. In this regard, my delegation recalls the recently adopted resolution on the trafficking of enslaved Africans, tabled by Ghana on behalf of the Africa Group. In conclusion, we are of the view that our collective credibility in addressing racism and racial discrimination is linked to our political will to confront such actors, guided by the Convention on Elimination of Racial Discrimination and the Durban Declaration and Programme of Action. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Ethiopia. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Bangladesh.

Mr. President, thank you for convening this important meeting. I also thank the facilitators for their hard work on the political declaration. Bangladesh aligns itself with the statement delivered by Uruguay on behalf of the G77 and China. 25 years ago, the Durban Declaration and Programme of Action made a clear promise: no one should face discrimination based on race, colour, descent, national or ethnic origin. Unfortunately, the world is far from achieving that goal. The DPA remains a vital framework. for Combating Racism, Racial Discrimination, Xenophobia and Related Intolerance. Bangladesh reaffirms its commitment to its full and effective implementation. As a diverse and developing country, Bangladesh is committed to equality, non-discrimination, human rights and the dignity of all. Guided by our commitment to transformative change, Our government is working to build a country free from poverty, hunger, exploitation, and discrimination. We are strengthening accountable governance and promoting the rights, dignity, and participation of women and marginalized communities. The recent launch of the Women-Centered Family Card and support for religious and ethnic communities are examples of this commitment. Mr. Preston, Bangladesh underscores the need to address historical and structural inequalities connected to slavery, colonialism, and other injustices. The responses must be people-centered, emphasizing justice, education, development, and international cooperation. We call for strong protection of the rights of migrants, refugees, forcibly displaced persons, minorities, women, children, and people in vulnerable situations. We must ensure that affected communities, including women and youth, are heard and meaningfully engaged in policymaking. We must all work together to ensure that new technologies promote sustainable development and counter, not proliferate, hatred and incitement to violence. The rapid development of AI confronts the world with both opportunities and threats. We need safe, secure, human rights-respecting AI with safeguards to ensure equality and non-discrimination. Bangladesh attaches great importance to international cooperation and multilateralism. We call on all States to strengthen cooperation with each other and with the United Nations and civil society. In conclusion, I reiterate Bangladesh's commitment to a world where diversity and dignity for all.
I thank the distinguished representative of Bangladesh. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of The Gambia.

The delegation of The Gambia welcomes the opportunity to reaffirm our commitment to the principles and objectives enshrined in the Durban Declaration and Programme of Action and its subsequent review and anniversary declaration. The Durban framework represents an important international commitment to confront racism, racial discrimination, xenophobia, and related intolerance in all their forms. It recognizes that these challenges are deeply rooted in historical, social, and cultural inequalities, and therefore require sustainable international cooperation and collective action. The Gambia reaffirms its commitment to leaving no one behind in advancing the 2023 agenda through international cooperation and multilateralism. We recognize that addressing inequality, discrimination, racism, xenophobia, hate speech, and intolerance require collective action and renewed commitment to human rights, equality, and sustainable development. Excellencies, across regions, We are witnessing troubling increase in xenophobia, anti-migrant sentiments, and racially motivated violence. The Gambia welcomes the progress made in combating racism and related intolerance. However, we remain concerned that these challenges persist in many parts of the world. We therefore call for renewed commitment and stronger collective action to address all forms of discrimination effectively and ensure that every individual can enjoy their rights and dignity. The Gambia welcomes the Second International Decade for People of African Descent as an important opportunity to advance recognition, justice, and development. The Gambia remains steadfast in strengthening national laws against discrimination, advancing justice reforms, and promoting inclusive education. To protect migrants and refugees within our borders, we continue to work with regional and international partners to protect vulnerable communities and foster peaceful coexistence. Our constituents obliges us to ensure that every person, Gambian and non-Gambian, enjoys equal protection and respect. Furthermore, the Gambia supports strengthened cooperation among states, the United Nations system, and all relevant stakeholders to eliminate racism, racial discrimination, xenophobia, and related intolerance. We also emphasize the importance of adequate resources and continued support for United Nations human rights mechanisms, including the Permanent Forum on People of African Descent, and to ensure effective implementation of their mandate. The DDPA reminds us of the enduring legacies of colonialism, slavery, apartheid and systemic racism. The Gambia underscores the importance of addressing this historical injustice through inclusive development, dialogue on reparatory justice, and empowerment of people of African descent worldwide. The Durban Declaration and Programme of Action remains a beacon of hope, a reminder that humanity falls.
I thank the distinguished representative of the Gambia. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of India.

Excellencies, the 25th anniversary of the adoption of the Durban Declaration and Programme of Action is an occasion not only for reflection, but also for renewing our collective resolve to eliminate racism, racial discrimination, xenophobia and related intolerance. Modern history bears witness to the immense suffering inflicted by doctrines of racial superiority, particularly through colonialism, slavery, and associated practices. While considerable progress has been achieved, these prejudices have not disappeared. They are resurfacing in new forms and are being amplified by digital platforms and emerging technologies. We are particularly concerned by the growing incidence of racist and xenophobic rhetoric directed against migrants and persons of foreign origin. Indians abroad, including students, professionals and workers, have also faced racial stereotyping, abuse and, in some cases, violence. Educational institutions, public discourse and digital spaces must foster mutual respect rather than normalize racial prejudice or hostility. States and digital platforms must act responsibly to prevent incitement to racial hatred and ensure accountability for racially motivated violence. India recently underwent its 21st to 23rd periodic review by the Committee of the Elimination of Racial Discrimination. India encouraged constructive engagement with the states confronting such trends and practical assistance to translate their obligations under the convention into effective national responses. Mahatma Gandhi's values continue to guide India's unwavering commitment to combating discrimination. Our constitution guarantees equality, prohibits discrimination on grounds including race, and provides safeguards for historically disadvantaged communities. India's multi-ethnic, multilingual, and multi-religious society demonstrates that diversity can be a source of strength. Effective implementation of the Durban Declaration requires education against racial prejudice, stronger national institutions, effective remedies for victims, and international cooperation supported by capacity building, finance, knowledge, and technology. Chair, humanity cannot advance through racial exclusion or notions of superiority. India will continue to support concrete, nationally led and internationally coordinated measures for the full and effective implementation of the Durban Declaration.

Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of India. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Mauritania.

Mr. President, Your Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, I am honored to participate on behalf of Mauritania in this high-level meeting on the occasion of the 25th anniversary since the adoption of the Durban Declaration and Programme of Action, we reiterate our firm commitment to address racism, racial discrimination, xenophobia, and related intolerance. The Durban Declaration and Programme of Action, since their adoption in 2001, have represented an important international framework to establish equality, dignity, and to protect the victims of discrimination, and to affirm the responsibility to address the historical reasons for injustice. Mr. President, Mauritania believes that addressing racism is not achieved through texts alone, but it requires public policies that are inclusive and that guarantee practical equality in enjoying rights and addressing the reasons for marginalization and that promote social justice and equal opportunity. In this context, my country has continued to develop its legislative framework for the protection of human rights. and has developed policies that aim to address all forms of discrimination and to address the legacy of slavery and human trafficking, and promoting access to social, cultural, and economic rights, including basic services, in particular, that benefit the most vulnerable segments. Mauritania has also adopted the National Strategy for the Promotion and Protection of Human Rights 2024 to 2028 as a framework to coordinate public policy in the area of human rights with the aim of firmly establishing the principles of equality, non-discrimination, justice, and the rule of law. We particularly believe in An education that promotes human rights and that promotes tolerance and acceptance of the other and strengthens the social fabric. Education is a necessary instrument in protecting against these scourges. Mr. President, the 25th anniversary -- the microphone has been cut off.
I thank the distinguished representative of Mauritania. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Singapore.

Mr. President, Madam Deputy Secretary-General, well, she just stepped out. 25 years ago, the international community came together in Durban and made a solemn commitment to confront racism, discrimination and intolerance. Today, that commitment is being tested more severely than at any juncture since 2001. Old prejudices are taking new ways to take root, as technology has been exploited as a tool to sow dissent, division and suspicion. It is precisely in this context that the Durban Declaration's call to action matters most. We must not let fear harden into hatred. History has shown us where that path leads. For Singapore, this is not an abstract concern. It is existential. We are a small, densely populated nation of immigrants, multi-ethnic, multi-religious, and highly interconnected. From our earliest days of independence, our leaders understood that survival depended on building something together. That conviction is enshrined in our National Pledge, adopted in 1966, to build a united nation and I quote, "regardless of race, language or religion". The harmony that Singapore enjoys today did not happen by accident. It is the result of decades of deliberate, sustained effort. Our Constitution affirms that all are equal before the law, regardless of race, language or religion. We regularly review our laws and policies to strengthen cohesion. Last year, we introduced a new Maintenance of Racial Harmony Act, adding community-based measures that strengthen reconciliation and bridge-building before tensions arise. Our public policies are designed to maximise the spaces where Singaporeans of different backgrounds live, learn and work together. We also partner with businesses, social enterprises and youth to run dialogues, ground-up projects and community events to foster social cohesion. These are the daily interactions to build mutual trust, respect and acceptance, brick by brick, year by year. Yet we know the work is never finished. Technology and AI have made it easier than ever to spread and amplify content that is designed to divide us. No country is immune, Singapore included. Singapore's response has been to combine firm legal safeguards, swift powers to act against harmful content wherever it originates, with sustained everyday investment in the dialogue that keeps trust between our races and faiths strong. Because when we choose to respect our differences and build genuine bridges, our societies grow stronger because of that diversity, not in spite of it. Mr. President, no country has all the answers. But we believe...
I thank the distinguished representative of Singapore. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Uruguay on behalf of the G77 and China.

Thank you, Mr. Chair. Excellencies, Distinguished delegates, I have the honor to deliver this statement on behalf of the Group of 77 and China. At the outset, allow me to thank the President of the General Assembly for convening this meeting, as well as the permanent representatives of Brunei Darussalam and Zimbabwe for their hard work throughout the negotiations of the political declaration considered adopted today. The Group of 77 and China has remained firmly committed to its foundational opposition to all forms of racism, racial discrimination, xenophobia, and related intolerance. As the core group presenting the annual resolution on the follow-up to the Durban Declaration and Programme of Action, we have a demonstrated history of commitment and support to this seminal and fundamental process. This high-level meeting convened to commemorate the 25th anniversary of the adoption of the Durban Declaration and Programme of Action offers an important opportunity to reaffirm its enduring significance as a landmark framework in our collective commitment to combating racism, racial discrimination, xenophobia, and related intolerance, and strengthen global support for the DPA and its implementation. The Durban Declaration and Programme of Action is not only about combating racism, racial discrimination, xenophobia and related intolerance. It is also about improving education and awareness, fighting poverty and marginalization, securing inclusive and sustainable development, reducing inequalities and respecting, protecting and promoting the human rights of all persons. Its relevance is further strengthened by the recognized nexus between combating racism, racial discrimination, xenophobia, and related intolerance and the achievement of sustainable development. The group also underscores the fundamental need to eliminate persistent historical and structural inequalities, particularly affecting women and girls, people of African descent, indigenous peoples, as well as local communities, including by acknowledging, addressing, and taking effective measures to remedy past tragedies and their consequences, such as affirmative policies and reparatory justice, and to eradicate all forms of discrimination. Moreover, in order to effectively eliminate racism and racial discrimination and eradicate negative stereotypes, we must educate today's children and young people about the history of racism and racial discrimination and their impacts, ensuring that future generations do not carry the weight of the past, either by perpetuating these harmful practices or by suffering their consequences. We remain deeply concerned about the alarming resurgence of all forms of racism in societies and call upon States to combat and oppose all forms of racism, including hate speech and religious intolerance, online and offline, worldwide, in line with the Durban Declaration and Programme of Action. It is also important to recognize the modern elements shaping racism and racial discrimination. Today, technology is developing at an unprecedented pace, while social media enables messages of hatred to spread at alarming speed, alongside misinformation and disinformation, increasingly amplified by artificial intelligence. New technologies can be extremely beneficial for sustainable development if used responsibly. We must work together to ensure that new developments contribute to a better world and do not perpetuate or exacerbate existing and structural inequalities. Mr. President, we will never achieve peaceful, just, and inclusive societies until we all begin to see and treat one another with equity. In this regard, I wish to conclude by reaffirming the group's unwavering commitment to the global fight against racism, racial discrimination, xenophobia, and related intolerance. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Uruguay on behalf of the Group of 77 and China. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Malawi.

Malawi aligns itself with the statement delivered on behalf of the Africa Group and the G77 and China. Twenty-five years after Durban, the Declaration remains the most comprehensive international framework for combating racism, racial discrimination, xenophobia and related intolerance. While progress has been made, these scourges continue to undermine peace, humanity, human dignity, social cohesion and sustainable socio-economic development. Their persistence reminds us that the objectives of the Durban Declaration are as relevant today as they were in 2001. Mr. President, recent events have demonstrated that xenophobia and racism remain a serious global challenge. Earlier this year, thousands of Malawian nationals were affected by xenophobic threats and violence, forcing many to abandon their homes, livelihoods, and businesses. The Government of Malawi undertook an extensive humanitarian and diplomatic response to facilitate a safe, orderly, and dignified voluntary retire, while engaging constructively with the regional partners in southern Africa to protect affected citizens and ensure safe transit. Mr. President, as Africa advances the vision of Agenda 2063, The free movement of people must be accompanied by a collective commitment to protect migrants from violence, discrimination and exploitation. No African should live in fear because of his or her nationality. The international community must also remain vigilant against emerging forms of racism and discrimination, including those amplified through digital platforms and new technologies. The principles enshrined in the Durban Declaration should guide our collective response to these evolving challenges. We, therefore, in conclusion, reaffirm our commitment to the full and effective implementation of the Durban Declaration and Programme of Action, and to strengthen international cooperation in eliminating racism, racial discrimination, xenophobia and related intolerance in all their manifestations.

I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Malawi. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Zambia.

Mr. President, distinguished delegates, today we mark the 25th anniversary of the Durban Declaration and Programme of Action, a landmark global commitment to confront racism, racial discrimination, xenophobia, and related intolerance in all their forms and manifestations. As we gather today to commemorate The adoption of this landmark declaration allow me to express my deep gratitude for the courage of the international community to name and confront what unjustly and disproportionately affects millions of people, particularly those of African descent. Indeed, the DDPA remains one of the most comprehensive and courageous frameworks ever adopted by the international community in its pursuit of equality, dignity, and justice for all. Yet, as we mark this important milestone, my gratitude is contrasted with profound sadness and sober reflection. This anniversary does not merely signify the passage of time, but it painfully reveals that we are 25 years late in achieving what is and should be the most basic expression of our shared humanity, the universal recognition and inherent respect for human dignity. Mr. President, An analysis of the Durban Declaration reveals that not only a moral vision, but a damning litany of the sources, causes, contemporary manifestations, and enduring consequences of racism and intolerance. Wisely, it remains from assigning blame, choosing instead of the higher path of collective responsibility and shared resolve for elimination of these scourges. It calls upon us to heal, to restore, and to rebuild fair and just societies grounded in equality. And yet, we must ask ourselves with honesty and urgency, what must it take for the international community to move decisively from rhetoric to reality? Perhaps progress has been hindered because the moral imperative to act rests solely on goodwill, and so it must. Coercion cannot and will not produce lasting peace or justice, and neither can complacency or selective commitment. True transformation demands sustained political will, accountability, resources, and above all, courage. The courage to confront uncomfortable truths and ultimately dismantle entrenched systems of inequality. Mr. President. The essence of the DDPA was never condemnation, but restoration. It sought to bring healing to historical wounds and to prevent their repetition. Today, as racism, xenophobia, and intolerance continue to persist and manifest in both old and new forms, we are once again confronted with the efficacy of our collective will. Let the 25th anniversary not be a moment of ceremonial remembrance alone.
I thank the distinguished representative of Zambia. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Trinidad and Tobago.

Trinidad and Tobago joins with the other concerned UN member states in applauding the efforts that have been made so far in highlighting the enduring structural and cultural influence of the transatlantic slave trade, which continues to exacerbate issues of inequality, underdevelopment, marginalization, and socioeconomic disparity throughout the developing world. As we mark the 25th anniversary of the adoption of the Durban Declaration and Programme of Action, I remind that Trinidad and Tobago proudly stands as a small but incredibly dynamic multicultural state with a unique sociopolitical and ethnic harmony. This is anchored in our constitution, which guarantees fundamental rights and freedoms without discrimination on the basis of race, religion, origin, or sex. In the spirit of the Durban Declaration mandate in 1985, Trinidad and Tobago was the first nation to proclaim a national holiday to commemorate the end of African enslavement through the celebration of African Emancipation Day. Trinidad and Tobago is also the first nation to declare a national holiday to commemorate the struggles of the spiritual Baptist community. This is nestled comfortably in a national calendar that also acknowledges the Hindu, Islamic, and Christian communities, which also exist due to the cut and thrust of the colonial era. The multicultural lines that are woven together to form a unique Trinbagonian tapestry compels our continued advocacy for action as outlined in the CARICOM's revised 10-point plan for reparatory justice and in furtherance of the full and effective implementation of the Durban Declaration and Programme of Action. Mr. President, as I conclude, As we can and as we continue to commend the good work that has resulted from Durban, we acknowledge the need for strengthened efforts to achieve global equality and heal the wounds of the past. For Trinidad and Tobago, we continue to strive to live by the words of our national anthem. Here, every creed and race find an equal place. I thank you, Chair.
I thank the distinguished representative of Trinidad and Tobago. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of the United Republic of Tanzania.

Mr. President, 25 years after the adoption of Durban Declaration and Programme of Action, its message remains as relevant as ever. Tanzania reaffirms its commitment to the elimination of racism, racial discrimination, xenophobia and related intolerance in all their forms. Despite progress, millions of people continue to face discrimination that denies them dignity, equality, and opportunity. New technologies and digital platforms must not become new channels for old prejudice. For Africa, the struggle against racial discrimination cannot be separated from the enduring legacy of slavery, the slave trade, colonialism, and apartheid. Their consequences continue to be reflected in inequalities within and among nations. Recognition of these historical injustices must therefore be accompanied by meaningful action. Tanzania supports constructive international engagement on reparatory justice and return of the cultural property, historical artifacts, and documents to their countries of origin, consistent with international law and agreed framework. Mr. President, Tanzania national identity is founded on unity, equality, and respect for human dignity. We are proud of our historic contribution to Africa's liberation and struggle against colonialism and apathy. At home, we have managed to overcome the colonial legacy of racism. The painstaking national building project we embarked on immediately after independence has paid off handsomely. Tanzania is today home to four races, at least three major world religions, and 120 tribes, weaved and lived together as one and speak one language, Swahili. We all regard ourselves as Tanzanians first and everything else second. Tanzania experience shows that it is possible, doable and achievable. And it's why we welcome the second International Decade for the People of African Descent as an opportunity to advance recognitions, justice and development. Mr. President, 25 years after Durban, our task is not to restate the promise of equality, but to deliver it. Let this anniversary move us from declaration to implementation, from acknowledgement to justice, and from inherited inequalities to a future shared dignity and equal opportunity. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of the United Republic of Tanzania. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Tunisia.

At the outset, I wish first and foremost to congratulate you on this 25th anniversary of the adoption of the Durban Declaration and Programme of Action. This is an important means of attainment of our common objective, namely combating racial discrimination and related forms of intolerance. Racism is not merely limited to traditional forms of prejudice. Today, we are bearing witness to discrimination within the working environment, within schools, and with the use of AI. In our international level response, we have a duty to take into consideration all of these components. Tunisia, in 2001, participated in the summit, a summit which resulted in the adoption of the Durban Declaration and Programme of Action. And we all were among the first states to adopt tangible measures in order to combat slavery. In 2018, UNESCO inscribed our program of fighting against slavery as part of the global memory program. At the national level, we have adopted a number of laws, laws geared towards combating racism. Our Tunisian constitution sheds light on equality in rights amongst citizens. Mr. President, Combating racism also requires that we tackle the root causes of this scourge and the historical causes thereof. Fighting against slavery and colonialism requires a recognition of the ramifications and repercussions thereof, and that these issues be incorporated into all programs, both at the national and international levels. For this reason, Tunisia renews its commitment to the declaration and the Djerba Declaration and Program of Action. We also wish to underscore the inalienable rights of the Palestinian people and the fight of the Palestinian people to restore these rights. We call upon the international community to shore up monitoring mechanisms for the Djerba Program of Action, inter alia, through tangible measures, first and foremost, equality and access to education and healthcare. Second, fighting against hate speech. And third, fighting against certain practices, and specifically the use of artificial intelligence and digital platforms for spreading hate speech. We need to continue to provide, to undertake efforts. The microphone was cut off.
I thank the distinguished representative of Tunisia. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Jamaica on behalf of the Caribbean Community.

Mr. President, I do have the honor to deliver this statement on behalf of the 14 member states of the Caribbean Community, and we align with the statement of G77 and China. CARICOM recognizes that while there has been some progress in its implementation since 2001, Much of the DDPAs promise remains unrealized and lacks the political will needed to unlock its true potential. As the most comprehensive international framework for addressing racism, racial discrimination, xenophobia and related intolerance, the DDPAs must continue to underpin our efforts in creating a fairer and more equitable world. We should not only proclaim that all human beings are equal in dignity and rights, but also demonstrate it. Today, we must regrettably acknowledge that racism, racial discrimination, xenophobia and related intolerance remain pervasive across the world. In some contexts, these manifestations have intensified and are increasingly amplified through digital technologies, including artificial intelligence systems. These contemporary challenges require a comprehensive and coordinated response, underpinned by decisive action by governments, private sector actors, and other relevant stakeholders to prevent and combat technology-facilitated racism and discrimination. Mr. President, CARICOM believes that in addressing our present challenges, we cannot diminish or overlook the significant impact of the legacies of the past. People of African descent continue to face the significant barriers to their advancement and development. deep-rooted structural and systemic racism continue to impede their full and equal participation in their societies, underscoring the urgent need for sustained efforts to dismantle the systems and practices that perpetuate inequality and discrimination. The persistence of racism against people of African descent is not coincidental. It is rooted in the historical injustices perpetrated against them during colonialism and the transatlantic trafficking in enslaved Africans, crimes against humanity recognized in the DDPA for which no remedy has yet been provided. CARICOM welcomes this long overdue recognition and the renewed momentum it has generated for the global reparatory justice movement. This updated plan builds on the previous iteration and provides a comprehensive framework for repairing the socioeconomic, cultural, psychological, and political legacies of the period of the transatlantic trafficking in enslaved Africans, native genocide, and colonization of our countries. It recognizes the persistent ills that the descendants of victims continue to face and presents a clear path forward to remedy these wrongs, including through a formal apology, restitution, compensation, and rehabilitation. CARICOM welcomes the proclamation of the Second International Decade for People of African Descent and sees it as an important opportunity to finally achieve recognition, justice, and development for people of African descent. Caricom calls upon all states to renew their commitment to the full and effective implementation of the DDPA and to translate that commitment into meaningful action. Mobilizing global public support for the implementation of the DDPA is fundamentally a call to advance human rights, dignity, equality and justice for all. Let us reaffirm our shared commitment to building a world in which every person, regardless of race, ethnic origin or nationality, is empowered to realize their full potential.
